description: Public, append-only, real-time log of every allocation call. Owned infrastructure.
tracked_config: Vero Compass v1.6.2 (12-asset pool including gold, up to 6 coins held, plus gold as a permanent hedge sleeve whenever it passes its own trend gate (so up to 7 positions), inverse-volatility sizing, BTC-trend crash filter − crypto moves to cash while the gold hedge is exempt and may stay held; the hedge is funded by selling the WEAKEST-ranked holdings rather than proportionally from all of them). Tracked from 2026-08-28; entries #1 and #2 were produced by v1.3/v1.4 − see engine_changes.

honesty.pool: The coin pool is a disclosed input, not a claimed edge. Curated-pool backtests are survivorship-biased and are never a performance headline. The forward log is the proof.
honesty.append_only: Never back-dated, never edited. A wrong call stays.

engine_changes.what_changed: When the book moves into the gold hedge, the money now comes from selling the weakest-ranked holdings instead of trimming every holding proportionally. Selection, pool, position count, sizing and the crash filter are unchanged.
engine_changes.why: On a survivorship-free test universe − one that keeps the coins which later went to zero − the change returns about 29% more with roughly 15 points less drawdown. That universe is the one that resembles live trading, because nobody knows in advance which coins survive.
engine_changes.what_it_does_not_improve: Measured instead on our curated 12-coin pool, the same change roughly HALVES the return and, across the full 2017-start window, improves drawdown by 0.1 points − that is, not at all. The reason is structural: those 12 coins are survivors, so the 'weakest holding' being sold is always a future winner and the rule only shows its cost. We consider the survivorship-free result the honest one, and we are publishing the unflattering one beside it rather than choosing whichever flatters.
engine_changes.known_cost: The benefit is concentrated in falling and choppy markets. Split by era, the new rule returned about 34% of the old one through the bull-dominated 2017-2021 stretch and about 141% through 2022-2026. If a strong alt season arrives, expect this version to lag the one it replaced. That is the trade being made deliberately, not an unexpected outcome.
engine_changes.drawdown_claim_scope: Lower drawdown is true from 2018 onward and strongly true after 2021. It is NOT true across the full 2017-start record on the curated pool. Any drawdown claim must name its period.
engine_changes.applies_to: Entries #1 and #2 were produced by v1.3/v1.4 and are unchanged. Entry #3 onward is produced by v1.6.

engine_changes.what_changed: Text only. An alert's Buy and Sell lines now name only coins that genuinely change hands: a coin fully used to fund the gold hedge is no longer listed as bought, and one the book held at zero is no longer listed as sold. The alert headline follows the same rule - EXIT when a real holding is sold, ENTRY when one is bought, REBALANCE when only the weights move.
engine_changes.why: Under v1.6, 94 of 154 historical alerts named at least one coin that did not actually change hands. The live alert of 2026-09-21 did it too: it listed LTC as a buy and XRP as a sell, and neither was traded.
engine_changes.what_it_does_not_change: When the system trades, and what it holds. Checked by comparing the indicator's complete year-by-year backtest table before and after the change: identical in every row.
engine_changes.known_limit: The alert is written at the close that triggers it and the trade is sized at the next open, so in roughly 1 fill in 10 a coin sitting right at the edge of zero can differ between the two. The 'Now hold' line remains the complete instruction.
engine_changes.applies_to: Everything from 2026-09-22 onward. Entries #1 to #3 are unchanged.

corrections.corrects: tracked_config, and the final sentence of engine_changes[0].what_changed, both published earlier today
corrections.what_we_published: That the book holds 'up to 6' positions, and that 'selection, pool, position count, sizing and the crash filter are unchanged' from v1.3/v1.4.
corrections.what_is_actually_true: Two things changed in v1.6, not one. Gold is now held as a permanent hedge sleeve whenever it passes its own trend gate, instead of having to win a top-6 momentum slot − so the book can hold up to 7 positions (6 coins plus gold) where before it held 6. And when the hedge is funded, the money comes from selling the weakest-ranked holdings rather than trimming every holding proportionally. Pool, base sizing (inverse-volatility), the crash filter, momentum length, trend gate and rebalance cadence are genuinely unchanged.
corrections.how_it_was_found: By reading the indicator's source after publication and confirming empirically that the book reaches 7 concurrent positions. The description had been written from research notes rather than from the code.
corrections.why_we_are_telling_you: We verify every published FIGURE against the data that produced it. This was a claim about how the mechanism works, in prose, and it went out with no such check because prose was not on the checklist. The indicator itself was correct throughout and no allocation, weight or logged call is affected − the error was in our description of it. The original wording is left in place above rather than rewritten, because a record that quietly edits its mistakes is not a record.

corrections.corrects: the allocation this page showed between 2026-08-31 and 2026-09-20
corrections.what_we_published: That the book was 100% gold — the allocation logged as call #2 on 2026-08-10.
corrections.what_is_actually_true: The tracked indicator changed allocation on 2026-08-30, out of 100% gold and into BTC, ETH, SOL and LINK alongside a gold hedge. Its alert fired on 2026-08-31 at 00:00 UTC and named the new book. Nobody wrote it down here, so for 21 days this page said 100% gold while the system held something else.
corrections.how_it_was_found: A check of the indicator's own panel against this log on 2026-09-20. The watchdog that should have caught it had been warning every day since 2026-08-21 about an unrelated label mismatch, so the day it had something real to say looked exactly like the twenty days before it.
corrections.what_it_cost_the_record: Measured with this repository's own method, from 2026-08-30 to the 2026-09-19 valuation, the allocation the system actually held returned +3.16% against the -2.51% of the gold the log still showed.
corrections.how_we_are_handling_it: Call #3 is logged today and counted from today. It is NOT back-dated to 2026-08-30. This record says it never back-dates, and the only thing a live log can prove is what it said at the time, so a window it did not publish does not count for us — whichever direction that window went.
corrections.why_we_are_telling_you: The alert worked. Delivery worked. What did not exist was the step that turns a fired alert into an entry here, and no amount of alarms fixes a missing step. The indicator's panel is now checked against this log every morning, and a difference is the only thing that raises a flag.

corrections.corrects: how the period between call #2 and call #3 was priced
corrections.what_we_published: Call #3 was logged on a Sunday. Gold has no session that day, so the gold period closed on the open of Friday 2026-09-18 - the session the entry names in its own detail - instead of on the next open after the call, which is how this record says it prices a close.
corrections.what_is_actually_true: The published figure reproduces exactly on the sessions the entry names, from public prices. But the same method re-derived once Monday's open exists resolves that boundary to Monday and gives a slightly different number. Two answers to one question is one too many.
corrections.how_it_was_found: Auditing our own publication, an hour after it went out.
corrections.how_we_are_handling_it: The entry stays exactly as published - not edited, not re-dated. verify.py now checks every entry against the sessions it named, with the prices still fetched from the public source and only the dates taken from the log, and prints whenever today's resolution would differ so the substitution is visible rather than silent. add_call.py now refuses to log a call whose period cannot close on a session at or after the call date, which is what should have stopped this one.
corrections.why_we_are_telling_you: The figure did not change and nobody was misled by it. We publish it because the alternative is a record that only discloses what somebody else might have caught.

corrections.corrects: the engine change of 2026-08-28 (v1.3/v1.4 to v1.6): the return and drawdown figures published with it
corrections.what_we_published: That on a survivorship-free test universe v1.6 'returns about 29% more with roughly 15 points less drawdown' than the engine it replaced, and that on our curated pool it 'roughly HALVES the return' and 'improves drawdown by 0.1 points'.
corrections.what_is_actually_true: The system rebalances on a fixed cycle, and the day that cycle happens to start on is arbitrary. Re-running the comparison on every possible start day shows the drawdown improvement holds on all of them, typically about 12 to 13 points. The return improvement does not: on a typical start day v1.6 returns about 9% LESS than the engine it replaced, and it trails on 13 of 21. The '29% more' we published came from one of the favourable start days. The costs we disclosed on the curated pool were overstated for the same reason - typically about 0.8x the return, not half. And one line was simply wrong: on the curated pool drawdown got 0.1 points worse (39.2% to 39.3%); it did not improve.
corrections.how_it_was_found: An audit of why the system scored better when trades were placed a day late. That traced the effect to the start-day dependence, and every figure we had published was then re-measured across all start days. None of the others was a favourable draw.
corrections.what_it_changes: Nothing about what the system holds or when it trades. It changes what we can claim for v1.6: better protection, not better returns.
corrections.why_we_are_telling_you: The claim that holds up is the one this product is built on - getting through the falls. The claim that did not is the one that would have sold it harder. Publishing only the first would be advertising.
